title: Mirrors
intro: Mirrors gives the speaker control over whose gaze counts. Other people's eyes are threatened, while his own reflection supplies flawless approval and prepares him for reporters. He calls this a role even as he names selfishness his true nature. The performance is therefore knowingly constructed, not a transparent record of uncomplicated self-love. A small appetite coupled with fear of hunger finally reveals the insecurity the grand image cannot remove. The return to the opening demands renews the defence rather than curing that fear.
reading: Control of scrutiny; role and claimed nature coexist; defensive self-admiration cannot guarantee material security.

revisions.t52-n2: He says he is deeply immersed in the role but not confused about it. That distinction puts the violent, vain persona on display as something performed with awareness. It also complicates the next claim that selfishness is his nature: the song alternates between costume and essence without settling which explains the other. Reading every threat or boast as a literal confession would miss the frame the lyric itself supplies.
revisions.t52-phrase-eyes: The early fantasy removes another person's eyes; the later gaze cannot turn away from the mirror. He rejects outside scrutiny while making his own looking the authority that declares him flawless. The prepared red carpet shows that he still wants to be seen, but on controlled terms. The issue is not simple invisibility. It is who is allowed to judge the image and what kind of judgement is permitted.
revisions.editorial-52-good-person: The claim that goodness has become impossible is justified by a private inventory of traps. That explanation makes the hardening understandable without making every subsequent act justified. The speaker can use injury both as a real memory and as permission to become less accountable. The song's acknowledgement of role-playing leaves that self-explanation open to inspection rather than presenting it as an unquestionable moral conclusion.
revisions.t52-phrase-appetite: He calls his appetite small and still fears not getting enough. The admission interrupts flawless self-regard and a public scene of success with a much more basic insecurity. Being able to stage importance does not guarantee provision. The opponent's waste then becomes especially offensive because it appears beside a need the speaker presents as modest. The repeated threats return after this fear, making them sound defensive as well as triumphant.
